title: Why Trend Following Works - Systematic Investor - Ep.391

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/Why Trend Following Works - Systematic Investor - Ep.391.docx

speakers: Rich Brennan (trend follower, Dunn, author The Fractals of Finance)
summary: Systematic Investor episode where Brennan presents empirical research from 68 futures markets since 1984: Hurst exponent 0.866, fat tails (tail exponent 3.33, five-sigma 5,791x too frequent) and volatility clustering (0.353) as evidence of structural feedback; applies it to the March 2026 crude oil spike. Conclusions: bell-curve risk and fixed vol targeting understate risk and trend following is structurally supported.

coverage.note: patience of models, hormuz barrels trapped
oil transmission to inflation, SocGen indices
short vs long-term indices; trend barometer; March performance
March moves, trend regime, pod shops; research design
fat tails, volatility clustering, convergent/divergent participants
vol targeting vs tails, agent-based threshold
inflation, rate cycle, recency bias, trend profitable even in bad regime

completeness_estimate: 0.85 - the first reader captured nearly every number and argument from Brennan's Hurst, tail and clustering research and the oil case study; it missed some secondary points (political management of energy prices, the stock-bond co-fall in March, Dunn's daily risk target, the two ways to harvest volatility expansion, trend followers' own role in the feedback loop).

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: The WTI fell from around 87 US dollars all the way down to roughly 66 US dollars over about 18 months.
claims.claim: WTI drifted down from about 87 to 66 dollars over roughly 18 months in an orderly decline before a sudden spike to about 119 dollars (+80%), a setup in which shorts built up and volatility was suppressed.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: Short interest had built up steadily. The market had been quiet long enough that the amplifying forces, the momentum traders, the the trend signals had largely stepped away.
claims.claim: Heavy short positioning, suppressed volatility and a long one-directional drift leave a market structurally coiled (dry undergrowth); a catalyst then triggers an outsized spike because momentum/amplifying participants had left.
claims.indicator: short interest / positioning, volatility, absence of trend signals
claims.conditions: after long quiet drift with crowded positioning
claims.testable: partly - positioning and vol compression measurable

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: that's a system that overshot with the participants who chased the spike getting stopped out, momentum signals flipping.
claims.claim: The 30% reversal from 119 to 84 within days is a position-driven overshoot unwinding as spike-chasers are stopped out and momentum signals flip.
claims.direction: fade after spike once participants stopped out

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: as soon as the pandemic came and was maybe in that case kind of the trigger, we saw inflation go up by 4 or 500% right from 2% to 10 11%.
claims.claim: The better inflation was managed during the 2010s, the larger the buildup for a consequential break (pandemic trigger took inflation from 2% to 10-11%), the same coiled-spring dynamic as oil.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: We never get tired. The models just wait. They they don't you know, even if it takes a year or even if it takes three years.
claims.claim: Trend models wait patiently; cocoa took about 15 years to deliver, so diversification of investment process matters for the 99% of portfolio that otherwise relies on opinions.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: it's about what you have in your portfolio when you're wrong. It's not just about being right.
claims.claim: Portfolios should be built for being wrong; trend following provides a non-correlated stream that pays off when forecasts fail.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: we've got about 20 million barrels per day trapped in that area. And 20 million barrels, that's actually the same amount that we saw in terms of demand destruction when the whole world closed down during the pandemic.
claims.claim: About 20 million bpd trapped by the Hormuz disruption equals the pandemic demand loss; as storage fills producers must cut output or shut refineries that are slow to restart, creating second-order effects.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: Prices go up fast and come down slowly.
claims.claim: Oil-driven cost increases pass through transport, manufacturing, food and wages, and prices are sticky downward (fuel surcharges are not cut), so inflation lingers after the commodity retraces; central banks tend to hike quickly, as the 1970s tolerance was costly.
claims.indicator: crude oil price, inflation, central bank response
claims.direction: oil spike raises inflation and rates

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: Those two scenarios have very different consequences for bonds, currencies, equities, central bank policy. But I suppose as trend followers, you and me needles, we don't need to decide this in in advance.
claims.claim: Trend followers need not decide whether a spike is a fundamental repricing or a positioning overshoot; they stay positioned to follow the confirmed trend.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: our SocGen trend following index uh hit a new all-time high at the end of February.
claims.claim: The SocGen Trend Index reached a new all-time high end Feb 2026 while the SocGen Short-Term Traders index recovered only about 50% of its drawdown; long-term strategies outperformed short-term ones, contrary to mid-2025 narrative.
claims.indicator: SocGen Trend Index vs SocGen Short-Term Traders index

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: My own trend barometer finished at 50 uh last night. Uh that's still a strong reading, uh meaning that there is fair fairly good breath in in a classical portfolio of trend following.
claims.claim: A trend barometer reading of 50 indicates good breadth of trends in a classical trend portfolio.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: trend followers, I would say most of them were on the right side of the move despite what you mentioned correctly is that trend uh sorry, oil uh had been in a downtrend for quite a while
claims.claim: Trend followers caught the oil spike because models flipped in mid-February; energy gains offset losses in equities, currencies and fixed income during early March 2026.
claims.indicator: trend signal change in crude oil

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Heating oil, to just give an example, despite the correction, it's still up 52% so far this month and crude is up around 40% from the end of February so far this month.
claims.claim: March 2026: heating oil up 52% and crude up 40% month to date while silver and platinum fell about 9%, likely from liquidations to raise cash.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: some of these quote-unquote multi pot shops or multi-strat funds or whatever has had a a little bit of a a tough time in March.
claims.claim: Multi-strategy pod shops struggled in March 2026 when tail events hit.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: you usually find that when you start getting into a market that's uh, exhibits these tail properties, uh, nearly all strategies fall over apart from um, the good old trend followers, um, long vol strategies
claims.claim: In regimes with fat-tail events (gold, metals, energy, deglobalization), most strategies fail except trend following and long-vol, making the coming regime beneficial for trend followers and hard for pod shops.
claims.direction: long trend following and long vol; avoid alternative styles

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: 68 uh, futures markets across eight different uh, classes. So we have equities, bonds, currencies, energies, metals, agriculturals using daily data uh stretching back to 1984.
claims.claim: The Fractals of Finance research tests whether trend patterns are a structural property of markets using 68 futures markets across 8 classes with daily data from 1984.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: If we find that trends do persist, that returns are not bell-shaped, and that volatile periods do cluster together, and if we find all three of these things simultaneously in every market we can study
claims.claim: Logic test: a memoryless market implies no persistence, normal returns and steady volatility; finding persistence, fat tails and volatility clustering together shows feedback is structural.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: the average Hurst exponent was not.5, it was 0.866.
claims.claim: Average Hurst exponent across 68 markets is 0.866 (decade averages 0.707 to 0.757), meaning long-range dependence in the scaling of price moves, present in every market and decade.
claims.testable: yes - Hurst estimation (but estimator sensitivity to sample size and bias is a caveat)

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: the directional correlation effectively averages out to zero. But this is this is something I'll reserve for the the later podcast with you. It's a very deceptive average.
claims.claim: Simple day-to-day directional autocorrelation averages near zero across large samples; the memory sits in the magnitude and clustering of moves, so trend works through volatility expansion out of calm, not daily autocorrelation.
claims.conditions: directional autocorrelation near zero on average but 'deceptive'

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: five sigma events occurred 5,791 times more frequently than the standard model predicts.
claims.claim: Five-sigma daily moves occur 5,791 times more often than a normal distribution predicts, with a power-law tail exponent of about 3.33 in every liquid market.
claims.indicator: five-sigma daily move frequency; tail exponent 3.33

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: we measured this using the auto correlation of the size of daily moves across all 68 markets, and the average was 0.353.
claims.claim: Volatility clustering is strong: the average autocorrelation of absolute daily move size is 0.353 across 68 markets.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: Value buyers, for example, arbitrageurs, mean reversion traders, they fit into this class of convergent trader. They produce the actual tall, narrow peak of the curve
claims.claim: Markets contain convergent (stabilising) participants creating the tall narrow peak of the distribution and divergent (amplifying) participants such as trend followers, momentum, stop-loss and margin calls creating the fat tails.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: as counterintuitive as it may sound, but we'll probably be selling oil the last few days in order to adjust our positions down within a certain risk framework.
claims.claim: Trend systems with dynamic position sizing reduce exposure as volatility expands, so they may sell during a spike and dampen rather than amplify; this differs from vol-buying approaches.
claims.conditions: dynamic position sizing, daily risk target

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: let's say you size positions to target a fixed volatility level. You're therefore implicitly assuming that recent volatility is a reasonable guide to future uh to the future.
claims.claim: Volatility targeting assumes recent vol predicts the future and is calibrated to the middle of the distribution; with tail exponent 3.33 it underestimates the chance of losses, e.g. oil sized for the calm 66-80 range then hitting 119.
claims.testable: yes - backtest vol targeting vs fixed risk

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: below a certain level of divergent participation, roughly 25 to 30% in the models that we applied, uh the simulated market behaves in a very stable way
claims.claim: Agent-based simulation shows a sharp threshold at roughly 25-30% divergent (amplifying) participation: below it markets are calm and bell-shaped; above it trends, volatility clusters and fat tails emerge.
claims.indicator: share of divergent participants in simulation

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: Regime changes are not random weather.
claims.claim: Trend/range regimes reflect the balance between stabilising and amplifying participants, driven by observable conditions (volatility, positioning, fear, momentum, margin levels); a quiet market is not evidence trend following stopped working, and strategies should be robust across regimes.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: the geopolitical shock was the catalyst that pushed participation above that threshold
claims.claim: The oil spike was a phase transition when the shock pushed amplifying participation above threshold; it reverted because the participant mix was not durably changed, and persistence depends on whether the supply disruption is real and sustained.
claims.direction: trend if sustained, revert towards mid-70s if resolved

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: Position sizing, value at risk calculations, stress tests calibrated to two or three sigma moves, all of these carry more exposure than they appear to.
claims.claim: Risk frameworks based on bell curves (position sizing, VaR, 2-3 sigma stress tests) understate risk; diversification across asset classes is participation in different feedback environments with the same structure.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: we've only had two periods now where we've had eight monthly winning month.
claims.claim: Dunn's record shows only two runs of eight consecutive winning months in 50 years; regimes can pay consistently once established, but 6-12 months of small monthly losses are normal while markets wait for a new regime.
claims.indicator: consecutive winning months in trend programme

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: if this oil move is sustained um the inflation is going to come roaring back.
claims.claim: A sustained oil spike would revive high inflation and interest rates (Australian cash 17.5% in the 1990s), producing significant trends and a healthy decade for trend following.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: we had, you know, 40 years of of of lower lows in in interest rates. Now we've started only recently, really, getting higher highs in interest rates.
claims.claim: Interest rates after a 40-year cycle of lower lows have started making higher highs, and rate regimes and the stock-bond correlation persist once established, so recency bias toward the old normal is dangerous.
claims.testable: partly - long cycles have few observations

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: even through the period where it wasn't necessarily conducive for trend following, we still made money.
claims.claim: Trend following was still profitable (though less so) in the unfavourable 2010s environment, so it is a robust strategy and not disaster insurance only.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: you had to be able to kind of imagine the unimaginable, right?
claims.claim: Risk planning has to include events that seem unimaginable; the oil spike from 66 to 119 followed by a 30% reversal is one visualisation of such an event, which standard risk models would treat as impossible.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: we know that the current administration, maybe even the previous administration, they would like to have lower energy prices, right?
claims.claim: Governments with an electoral incentive manage energy prices lower (political agenda, intervention); this can hold prices down for a while, but when it stops working the market reasserts itself sharply, adding to the coiled-spring build-up in oil.
claims.direction: oil spike risk after managed low prices
claims.conditions: works only until policy management fails

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: aggregate bond index in the US is down 1.21%, so no help from from bonds
claims.claim: In early March 2026 the oil shock hit stocks (MSCI World about -2.8% month to date, flat for the year) and bonds (US aggregate about -1.2%) together, so bonds gave no hedge; the SG CTA and Trend indices fell only about 2.1% on the month and were still up about 6.1% for the year, with energy gains offsetting equity, currency and fixed income losses.
claims.indicator: MSCI World, US aggregate bond index, SG CTA and Trend index returns (Mar 2026)
claims.direction: trend index loses less than stocks; bonds fail as hedge in an oil-driven inflation shock
claims.conditions: energy supply shock with positive stock-bond correlation
claims.testable: yes - index returns for the month checkable

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: the conditions which sustain a trend, elevated volatility, clustering of moves in one direction, amplifying participant behavior, tend to persist once they're established.
claims.claim: Trend following works not because each day's direction predicts the next but because the conditions that sustain trends (high volatility, one-directional clustering, amplifying participants) persist once established; the market does not reset to a blank slate each day.
claims.direction: trend continuation once volatility regime is established
claims.testable: partly - regime persistence and conditional trend returns testable

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: something that can't be arbitraged away as easily because it's not a simple signal you can trade on
claims.claim: The memory captured by the Hurst exponent is a property of the price process (energy accumulation, volatility clustering, persistence of a trending state) rather than a simple daily directional signal, so it cannot be arbitraged away as easily as directional autocorrelation.
claims.testable: partly - persistence of the structural property over time is testable, the non-arbitrage claim is an argument

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: We are participants in the feedback system itself that generate the very phenomena we exploit.
claims.claim: Trend followers are not external observers: as divergent (amplifying) participants they are part of the feedback system that creates the fat tails and trends they profit from, so trend following is alignment with a structural feature of price formation rather than just a style.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: expansion by buying cheap vol and sell it when you get out. But but you can also do it um in a more mechanical way like we do.
claims.claim: Volatility expansion can be harvested two ways: buying cheap volatility and selling it on the spike (the Dave Dredge approach) or mechanically via trend following with dynamic position sizing; the difference lies in how position size is treated as vol rises.
claims.direction: long cheap vol vs trend following with vol-scaled sizing
claims.testable: partly - compare payoffs of long vol and vol-sized trend around vol spikes

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: at Dawn at least we use we use a daily risk target. Not a daily volatility target.
claims.claim: Dunn targets a daily risk level rather than a fixed volatility target, while many managers still use a fixed volatility target; the host argues this distinction matters because of the fat-tailed return distribution.
claims.indicator: daily risk target vs fixed volatility target
claims.conditions: fat tails make a fixed vol target unreliable
claims.testable: partly - compare drawdown of risk-target vs vol-target sizing

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: that's the empirical basis for conviction in trend following signals even when the positions feel uncomfortable for us.
claims.claim: Because trend memory (Hurst 0.866) is a persistent structural feature, trend signals are not noise that dissolves on inspection, which gives an empirical basis for holding trend positions with conviction even when they are uncomfortable.
claims.testable: no - argument for conviction, not a test

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: if the geopolitical situation resolves, the stabilizing forces reassert and prices return towards the mid-70s.
claims.claim: Conditional oil view: if the geopolitical situation resolves, stabilising participants reassert and WTI returns toward the mid-70s; if the disruption is sustained, the new price level builds its own structural support and the spike becomes a genuine trend rather than a spike-and-revert.
claims.direction: WTI to about mid-70s if resolved; persistent trend if sustained
claims.conditions: depends on whether the supply disruption is real and persistent
claims.testable: yes - price path versus the two scenarios
